title: Questions it has not seen
objectives: Score a model on examples it was not fitted on, and say why a perfect score on its own examples proves little.

screens.title: Which looks better?
screens.prose: Two models of the ten training emails. The **memoriser** stores every email and gives back its label. The rule is **spam when links are at least 5**.

state.caption: The memoriser looks up each email's own stored label.

screens.question: Which scores better on these ten training emails?

options.text: The memoriser, 10 of 10
The rule, 9 of 10
options.why: The rule misses the spam email with 2 links. The memoriser gets that one too.

options.text: They tie
options.why: Count again: the memoriser repeats every label, the rule misses one.

hints.text: The memoriser just repeats the labels it stored.
It cannot be wrong on emails it stored: 10 of 10.

feedback.correct: On its own examples the memoriser is perfect: 10 of 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count each model's right answers on the training rows.

explain.text: The memoriser gives back each stored label, so it scores 10 of 10. The rule gets 9. Whether that makes the memoriser better is the question of this lesson.

screens.title: New emails
screens.prose: Six new emails arrive. They were kept back: neither model saw them while it was being built. Fill in what the rule says for each.
screens.question: Type yes or no for each new email: does the rule say spam?

hints.text: The rule says yes when links are at least 5.
4 links is below 5.
no, no, no, yes, yes, yes.

feedback.correct: The rule says no, no, no, yes, yes, yes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each link count with 5.

byKey.r2c2: 4 is below 5, so the rule says no, although this email is spam.

explain.text: The rule says spam for 5, 8 and 10 links. It is wrong only on the email with 4 links. That is 5 of 6 right.

screens.title: The memoriser meets new emails
screens.prose: The memoriser looks up each new email's link count among the training emails. It has never seen 8 or 10.
screens.question: How many of the six new emails can the memoriser answer at all?

hints.text: Which new link counts appear among the training emails?
0, 2, 4 and 5 do; 8 and 10 do not.

feedback.correct: It can answer 4; it has nothing to say about 8 or 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the rows that are not “never seen”.

byKey.all: Two rows say never seen. The memoriser has no answer there.
byKey.right: 2 is how many it gets right. It answers 4.

explain.text: The memoriser only knows emails it stored. Counts 8 and 10 never appeared, so it answers 4 of the 6.

screens.title: Training and test
screens.prose: Data used to choose the rule is **training data**. Data kept back, never used to choose, is **test data**. A model is judged on the test data.
screens.question: Of the 4 new emails the memoriser answers, how many does it get right?

hints.text: Compare the Memoriser column with Spam on the first four rows.
2 links: it says yes, but the email is not spam.

feedback.correct: Only 2 right: the emails with 0 and 5 links.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two columns row by row.

byKey.answered: 4 is how many it answers. Only 2 of those match the label.
byKey.all-test: 6 is the number of test emails. Count only the matches.

explain.text: It is right on 0 and 5 links and wrong on 2 and 4. So the perfect memoriser gets 2 of 6 test emails right, while the rule gets 5.

screens.title: The test score
screens.prose: The rule gets 5 of the 6 test emails right.
screens.question: What share is that, as a percentage to one decimal place?

hints.text: Divide 5 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the right answers by 6.

byKey.train: 90% is the training score. The test score uses the six new emails.

explain.text: 5 right out of 6 is $\tfrac{5}{6} \approx 83.3\%$. That, not the 90% on training emails, is the honest score.

screens.title: Pick a model
screens.prose: Two spam models were built by different teams. Each was scored on its own training data and on the same test data.
screens.question: Which model should the company use?

options.text: B: it scores better on the test data
A: it scores better on its training data
options.why: A's 98% is on emails it was built from. On new emails it gets 71%.

options.text: A: its average of the two is higher
options.why: Averaging mixes in the training score, which proves little. Judge on test data.

options.text: Neither, until both score 100% on training
options.why: 100% on training is easy for a memoriser and says nothing about new emails.

hints.text: Which column tells us about emails neither model saw?
Test: B 82% against A 71%.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the column for data neither model was built from.

byKey.a: You chose by the training score. A probably memorised its training data: it drops to 71% on new emails.

explain.text: Training scores flatter the model that memorises. On test data B gets 82% and A 71%. Use B.

screens.title: Tuning on the test
screens.prose: A colleague tries every threshold on the six test emails. At $t$ = 3 the rule gets all six right, so they report a test score of 100%.
screens.question: What is wrong with the 100%?

options.text: The test emails chose $t$, so they no longer test it
Nothing is wrong: the rule is right on all six
options.why: It is right on the six it was tuned to. That is a training score in disguise.

options.text: Six emails are far too few to score anything
options.why: Six is small, but the real fault is that they were used for choosing.

options.text: $t$ = 3 is simply a worse rule than $t$ = 5
options.why: Which $t$ won is not the point. Once the test emails choose, the score is no longer a test.

hints.text: What makes test data a fair test?
It must never be used to choose the rule.

feedback.correct: Choosing on the test set turns it into training data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the six emails helped choose the rule.

byKey.fine: You trusted the score. The six emails picked $t$ = 3, so scoring on them again is marking your own homework.

explain.text: A test set is honest only if it played no part in choosing. Here it chose $t$ = 3, so 100% says as little as the memoriser's 10 of 10. A fresh test set is needed.

screens.title: A test of two
screens.prose: Another team tests two thresholds on just two kept-back emails. Both models get both right.
screens.question: What does this test tell us about which model is better?

options.text: Almost nothing: two emails cannot split them
They are equally good models on all emails
options.why: They tie on two emails. On many new emails they could differ a lot.

options.text: Both are perfect models, with nothing to fix
options.why: 2 of 2 is a tiny sample. One more email could drop either to 2 of 3.

hints.text: How many test emails would the two rules disagree on?
Only emails with exactly 4 links separate $t$ = 4 from $t$ = 5; neither test email has 4.

feedback.correct: Two emails are too few to separate them.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how small the test is.

explain.text: The rules differ only on emails with exactly 4 links. Neither test email has 4, so the test cannot see the difference. More test examples usually help.

screens.title: What a score means
screens.prose: A model is only as good as its score on questions it has not seen. $$\text{test score} = \dfrac{\text{right on kept-back examples}}{\text{kept-back examples}}$$ A perfect training score proves little: a memoriser always has one.
screens.question: A model scores 100% on 500 training rows and 70% on 200 test rows. Which number goes in the report?

options.text: 70%, on the test rows
100%, on the training rows
options.why: That is the score on rows the model was fitted to, which a memoriser would also reach.

options.text: 85%, the average
options.why: Averaging mixes in the training score.

hints.text: Which rows did the model never see?
The 200 test rows: 70%.

feedback.correct: 70%, the score on rows it never saw.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Report the score on kept-back rows.

explain.text: The 100% only says the model fits what it was built from. The 70% on unseen rows is what to expect next.

screens.title: The backtest that failed
screens.prose: A trader tries thirty rules on 2019 to 2022 and keeps the one that made the most money: £84,000 on paper. Run on 2023, it loses £12,000.
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The same years chose the rule and scored it
2023 was just an unlucky year for the rule
options.why: Maybe, but the £84,000 was never a fair test: the same years chose the rule and scored it.

options.text: Thirty rules were too few to try first
options.why: Trying more rules on the same years makes the paper profit even less honest.

options.text: The paper profit was simply miscounted
options.why: The sum can be right and still prove little, because those years picked the rule.

hints.text: Which years chose the rule? Which years scored it?
Both were 2019 to 2022, so the £84,000 is a training score.

feedback.correct: The same years chose and scored the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the years that scored the rule were kept back.

explain.text: The £84,000 is a training score: the years that picked the rule also scored it. 2023 was the first real test, and the rule failed it. Later courses treat this properly.

ideas: Training data chooses the rule; test data is kept back and used only to score it.
A memoriser scores 100% on its own examples and has nothing to say about new ones.
Choosing the rule again on the test data turns it into training data, and the score stops meaning anything.

formula.name: Test score
formula.note: Score once, on examples that played no part in choosing.

summary.trap: Reporting the training score, or tuning on the test set, makes a model look better than it is.

quiz.prose: A model gets 18 of 24 test examples right.
quiz.question: What is its test score, as a percentage?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the right ones by 24.

byKey.count: You typed the count 18 as a percentage. Divide by 24 first.

quiz.prose: A program stores all 1,000 training emails and answers with each one's label.
quiz.question: Its training score is 100%. What does that tell us about new emails?

options.text: Very little: storing labels is not learning a rule
It will be about 100% on new emails too
options.why: It has no rule for emails it never stored, as the memoriser had none for 8 links.

options.text: It will be bad on new emails
options.why: We cannot say it will be bad either. Only a test set can tell.

feedback.correct: A perfect training score proves little.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think of the memoriser.

explain.text: Any program that stores the labels scores 100% on them. Only kept-back examples show how it does on new emails.

quiz.prose: You have 100 labelled emails and want an honest score for a threshold rule.
quiz.question: Which plan is right?

options.text: Choose $t$ on 80 emails, then score it once on the other 20
Choose $t$ on all 100, then score it on all 100
options.why: Then every email chose the rule; the score is a training score.

options.text: Choose $t$ on 80, score on 20, then choose again on the 20
options.why: Choosing on the 20 makes them training data too.

options.text: Choose $t$ on 20 and score it on the same 20
options.why: The same emails chose and scored the rule.

feedback.correct: Keep 20 back, choose on 80, score once.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The scored emails must play no part in choosing.

explain.text: The 20 kept-back emails must never touch the choice. Scored once, they give an honest estimate for new emails.
